planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant nursery stock in spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ethiopian highland growers traditionally train it as a hedge or small tree and harvest leafy twigs rather than fruit.

directions: Gesho is an evergreen shrub of the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands whose bitter leaves and twigs serve the same role in traditional tej (honey wine) and talla (sorghum beer) brewing that hops serve in European beer, imparting bitterness and helping preserve the ferment. Growers typically coppice or hedge the shrub, harvesting young leafy branches that are dried, crushed, and added directly to the fermenting must or brewed into a bitter tea first. It tolerates a range of soils but grows fastest in fertile, well-drained ground with regular moisture, and establishes readily from cuttings taken from a productive mother plant. Where winters are too cold for reliable outdoor survival, it can be container-grown and overwintered under cover, since hard frost will kill topgrowth.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization — traditional African fermented beverages
International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA)

planting.note: Transplant nursery-raised seedlings into rich, well-drained, high-organic-matter soil in filtered shade once frost risk has fully passed, mimicking the forest-shade coffee gardens of the Ethiopian highlands.

directions: Unlike the single-clone cultivars bred elsewhere, Ethiopian Heirloom is an industry shorthand for the enormous, genetically diverse complex of unselected Coffea arabica landraces still growing semi-wild or in forest-garden cultivation across Ethiopia's highlands, the species' birthplace. Trees raised from Ethiopian heirloom seed show far more variation in leaf shape, bean size, and cup character than named commercial cultivars, which is part of why specialty roasters prize regionally labeled lots like Yirgacheffe and Sidamo rather than a single varietal name. Grow seedlings under high, filtered shade with rich, slightly acidic, humus-laden soil and steady moisture, replicating the understory conditions of a traditional Ethiopian forest coffee garden. Expect the first useful harvest only after three to four years, with full production building over the following several seasons.
sources: Specialty Coffee Association — origin and varietal reference
World Coffee Research — Arabica Coffee Varieties catalog

planting.note: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 55°F; Georgian cooks traditionally pick the fruit green for pickling rather than letting it ripen red.

directions: Tsitsaka is a mild, thin-walled, elongated pepper that is the traditional centerpiece of Georgian pickled-pepper preparations such as tsitsaka turshi, served as a staple accompaniment to supra feast tables. The fruit is harvested green and slightly immature, when the walls are at their crispest and most suited to brining with garlic, dill, and vinegar. Grow it like a standard bell-type pepper in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, providing consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot and bitter fruit. Because the variety is grown specifically for pickling rather than fresh eating or drying, harvest continuously through the season rather than waiting for fruit to color, which keeps plants productive longer.
sources: Georgian National Agricultural University — traditional vegetable varieties

planting.note: Raise seedlings in a flooded nursery bed and transplant into puddled, flooded paddy soil once soil temperature is reliably above 70°F, maintaining shallow standing water through most of the vegetative season.

directions: Thadokkham 1 is a widely grown lowland glutinous rice released by Laos's National Agriculture and Forestry Research Institute (NAFRI) to give farmers a higher-yielding, more uniform alternative to older sticky-rice landraces while keeping the soft, sticky texture central to Lao cuisine, where glutinous rice is the daily staple eaten by hand. Farmers transplant seedlings by hand into puddled wet paddies and maintain shallow standing water through tillering and heading, draining the field only as the grain approaches maturity. The cooked rice is notably soft and cohesive even after cooling, suited to the traditional method of steaming in a conical bamboo basket rather than boiling. Because it is a lowland wet-season variety bred for Laos's monsoon climate, it needs a long, warm, reliably flooded growing season to perform well.
sources: Lao National Agriculture and Forestry Research Institute (NAFRI)
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) — variety release records

planting.note: Plant seed tubers a few weeks before to shortly after the last frost into deep, loose, well-drained soil; this long-season Andean landrace needs a cool growing season and more time to mature than standard commercial potatoes.

directions: Papa Huayro is one of the most recognizable Peruvian native potato landraces, prized for its elongated, irregular tubers streaked with purple over a cream background and for a dense, slightly dry, intensely flavorful flesh that holds its shape well in cooking. It is a traditional ingredient in classic Peruvian dishes such as papa a la huancaina and pachamanca, where its firm texture and rich flavor are considered superior to modern commercial potato varieties. Grow it in deep, loose, well-drained soil with cool growing-season temperatures similar to its high-Andean origin, hilling the developing tubers as the plant grows to protect them from sun greening. Because it is a long-season landrace rather than a modern bred cultivar, expect a longer time to maturity and more variable yields than standard potato varieties.

planting.note: Plant seed tubers around the last frost into deep, loose, well-drained soil; this diploid Andean species is distinct from common tetraploid potatoes and performs best in a cool growing season with moderate day length.

directions: Papa Amarilla belongs to a separate diploid potato species distinct from the common tetraploid Solanum tuberosum, and is the classic potato used for causa limeña, the layered Peruvian dish that relies on its intensely yellow, dense, dry-textured flesh to form a moldable mashed base. The tubers are smooth-skinned, pale yellow, and notably starchy with very little watery texture, a quality cooks specifically seek out for dishes where the potato must hold a shape rather than remain creamy. Grow it the same way as other Andean potato landraces, in deep, loose, well-drained soil under cool growing conditions, hilling as tubers develop to prevent greening. Because it is a diploid species adapted to high-altitude Andean day length and temperature, yields and performance can be less predictable at low elevation or in long, hot summer days.
